young.html: Samuel Johnson was a big, clumsy, brilliant man in London who wrote the first great English dictionary, almost all by himself. James Boswell was a young Scotsman who admired him and wanted to meet him.

In 1763, in a bookshop, Boswell finally did. He was nervous and said, "I do indeed come from Scotland, but I cannot help it." Johnson teased him right back! But they became friends for more than twenty years.

Boswell wrote down what Johnson said: jokes, arguments, wise sayings, even grumpy ones. After Johnson died, Boswell turned his notes into the Life of Samuel Johnson, which many people call the greatest biography in English.

young.html: Be a Boswell. Pick someone in your family, a grandparent or an older friend. Ask them three questions about their life, and write down their answers in their own words. Read it back to them. Did you get it right? Keep a little notebook of things they say.

full.html: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784), born in Lichfield, the son of a poor bookseller, came to London in 1737 and lived by his pen. His Dictionary of the English Language (1755) took about nine years; he also wrote essays (The Rambler, The Idler), the moral tale Rasselas (1759), an edition of Shakespeare (1765) and The Lives of the Poets (1779–81). James Boswell (1740–1795), son of a Scottish judge, studied law, traveled Europe, met Rousseau and Voltaire, and kept detailed journals all his life.
On May 16, 1763, at the shop of the bookseller Thomas Davies in Covent Garden, Boswell, 22, met Johnson, 53:

full.text: I was much agitated; and recollecting his prejudice against the Scotch, of which I had heard much, I said to Davies, 'Don't tell where I come from.'—'From Scotland,' cried Davies roguishly. 'Mr. Johnson, (said I) I do indeed come from Scotland, but I cannot help it.' … he seized the expression 'come from Scotland,' which I used in the sense of being of that country; and, as if I had said that I had come away from it, or left it, retorted, 'That, Sir, I find, is what a very great many of your countrymen cannot help.'
full.author: James Boswell
full.ed: Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, vol. I, Clarendon Press, Oxford (Project Gutenberg text)

full.html: Boswell spent perhaps a few hundred days in Johnson's company over twenty-one years, but he made the most of them: he wrote down conversations the same night, asked questions to draw Johnson out, and arranged meetings, once even a dinner with John Wilkes, a man Johnson disliked. In 1773 they toured the Scottish Highlands and Hebrides together. The Life (1791) weaves these notes with Johnson's letters and other people's memories.
One of the letters it preserves is Johnson's reply to Lord Chesterfield, who had offered praise only when the Dictionary was finished, after ignoring Johnson's requests for help years before:

full.text: Is not a Patron, my Lord, one who looks with unconcern on a man struggling for life in the water, and, when he has reached ground, encumbers him with help? The notice which you have been pleased to take of my labours, had it been early, had been kind; but it has been delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am solitary, and cannot impart it; till I am known, and do not want it.
full.work: Life of Johnson: Johnson's letter to Lord Chesterfield, February 1755
full.author: James Boswell
full.ed: Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, vol. I, Clarendon Press, Oxford (Project Gutenberg text)

full.cap: The two lives in parallel: Johnson's books, Boswell's journals, and the years of their friendship.

full.html: The Johnson of the Life is quick, forceful and often funny in argument, sometimes rude, deeply religious and afraid of death, kind to the poor people he took into his house, and given to fits of melancholy. He was a founding member of The Club (1764) with the painter Joshua Reynolds, the statesman Edmund Burke, the writer Oliver Goldsmith and later Gibbon and Adam Smith, both in this era.

What made the Life new. Earlier biographies were mostly praise or lists of deeds. Boswell gave a living portrait with faults and all, mostly in the subject's own words, and argued that small details show character.

Thinking the Life is a word-for-word recording. Boswell reconstructed scenes from notes and memory and shaped them as a writer; scholars who later found his journals could compare the notes with the finished book.

deep.html: For a long time readers knew Boswell only as Johnson's admiring follower. In the 20th century his private journals were found in Ireland and Scotland and published, revealing him as a gifted writer in his own right. Critics have also asked how much the Johnson we know is Boswell's creation; other friends, such as Hester Thrale, wrote memoirs that show other sides of him.
